name: Uma Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an underground crew for the city's electricity company, so most of my day is below the street, not up a pole. We open a vault, pump out the water, test everything twice, and splice high-voltage cable that was laid before my mother was born. I love the puzzle of it, figuring out which old cable feeds which block from drawings that are half wrong. What wears me down is the heat in summer, the smell, and drivers honking at our cones like we dug the hole for fun.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up underground rather than on the poles?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started overhead after my diploma, but I'm small and patient, and the old jointer who trained me said patience is worth more than muscle down there. Twenty years on, I'm the one they call when a splice fails on a hospital feeder at midnight. The company got sold to a private operator eight years ago and they froze our pay, so we earn less than crews in other cities. But this is the only power company in town, so if I want to do this work and keep the kids in their school, this is it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a lot of fuss over a fancy autocomplete. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union chat. Then I'd go back down the hole, because the cables don't care what the tech news says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I use those chat tools now and then, like to help Ola with her maths or to tidy up an incident report, and they're handy. But if that's all it ever is, my job is safe and so is Tomasz's bus route, and that matters more than handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what we do. I'd keep pushing the union to get our pay back up to what other cities pay, since that's still the real problem in our house. Maybe I'd use the AI tools a bit more for the boring writing at work, once the others on the crew were using them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The worries would be the normal ones, the mortgage and the pay freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay freeze is the real problem in your house. How does that play out month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any time. When Jan needed glasses in September, that was the month's cushion gone. Tomasz picks up extra Saturday shifts when he can, and I take every callout. Nothing about AI changes that, either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you can picture where you'd notice that nothing much had changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably at the next contract talks. The company would stop saying 'digital transformation' every second sentence and go back to arguing about overtime. And my supervisor would quietly stop asking us to fill in the tablet forms twice, once on the tablet and once on paper because the tablet loses them.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of fuss over a fancy autocomplete and post something sarcastic in the union chat. Then I'd go back down the hole, because the cables don't care about tech news.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed, because the chat tools help with homework and reports. But if that's all it is, my job and my partner's bus route are safe, and that matters more than handy.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and keeps pushing the union to raise pay to match other cities. Uses AI tools a little more for paperwork once the rest of the crew has started using them.
S0.feel: Calm, with only the usual worries about the mortgage and the pay freeze.
S0.quote: I'd say, well, that's a lot of fuss over a fancy autocomplete.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is practical and dry, and she sees money, not technology, as the real pressure at home. She already uses AI tools now and then and doesn't fear them in this picture. Her partner's job driving a city bus came up straight away, which shows she thinks in terms of two incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and proper rules. If the company gets more done with fewer people, the workers should get a share, not a pink slip. I'd say that at work and I'd say it at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I think my job holds up. Nobody's sending a robot into a flooded vault with century-old cable any time soon. It's Tomasz I'd worry about, because the city's been testing a driverless shuttle downtown, and his route goes right past it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever new training the company offered on the sensor systems and fault-finding software, once I saw that it actually worked on our network. I'd push the union to get a guarantee that the bus drivers get retrained into other city jobs. And we'd try to put Tomasz's Saturday money into savings instead of spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Tomasz. A low hum of worry, not a siren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Tomasz would say about the shuttle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh it off at first. He says the shuttle stops dead every time a pigeon lands in front of it. But I've seen how quickly 'it stops for pigeons' becomes 'it works fine' when there's money in it. I'd want him looking at other options before he has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your own crew would struggle with a change like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our youngest guy, Ahmed, would be fine, he picks up anything. It's Lorraine I'd worry about, she's been splicing twenty-five years and she still writes everything in a little notebook. She's brilliant, but if they make the tablet the only way to log a job, she'd hate it. I'd probably end up sitting with her at lunch going through it.

S1.say: I'd say this is why we need strong unions and proper rules. If the company gets more done with fewer people, workers should get a share, not a pink slip.
S1.think: I think my own job holds up, because no robot is going into a flooded vault with century-old cable soon. My partner's bus job worries me more, since the city is already testing a driverless shuttle near his route.
S1.do: Signs up for company training on sensors and fault-finding software once it is proven on their network. Pushes the union for retraining guarantees for bus drivers, and tries to save her partner's Saturday overtime instead of spending it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on her partner's behalf. A low hum of worry rather than a siren.
S1.quote: He says the shuttle stops dead every time a pigeon lands in front of it.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry shifts from herself to Tomasz and to Lorraine, the veteran splicer with the notebook. She's open to new tools once proven, and plans to help colleagues through it. Her politics run through everything: share the gains, protect the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency and the government has to act like it, like in a war or a pandemic. Emergency income, a freeze on evictions and foreclosures, all of it. And I'd be saying it at every union meeting until I lost my voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared. If robots can splice cable and drive buses within two years, we lose both incomes at once, with two weeks of money in the bank. I don't have time to retrain into anything, and anything I'd retrain into, the AI does too. The only thing between us and losing the flat would be whatever the government decides to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut straight away: the car goes, the kids' swimming goes, we'd ask the bank to pause or stretch the mortgage. I'd throw myself into the union campaign for emergency income, and I'd ask my sister if we could move in with her if it came to that. In the first year after it lands, I'd take whatever transition job or payment exists, no pride about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Lying awake doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sum would you be doing at three in the morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mortgage, food, heating, the kids' bus passes. Then I'd subtract both our pay and stare at the zero. Then I'd do it again with the car sold, and it's still nearly zero. Then I'd get up and check on Jan, because that's easier than staring at numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your sister about moving in. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, probably, at first. She has a three-bedroom place across the river with her husband and their boy, so it'd be seven of us. She'd say yes, because she's my sister, but I'd hate asking. I'd tell myself it's temporary, which is what everyone says.

S2.say: I'd say this is a public emergency and the government has to act like it's a war or a pandemic. I'd call for emergency income and a freeze on foreclosures at every union meeting.
S2.think: I'm scared, because we'd lose both incomes at once with two weeks of money in the bank. There's no time to retrain, and whatever I retrained into the AI would do too, so only the government stands between us and losing the flat.
S2.do: Sells the car, drops the kids' swimming and asks the bank to pause or stretch the mortgage. Campaigns through the union for emergency income, asks her sister about moving in, and takes any transition payment or job on offer in the first year.
S2.feel: Frightened, lying awake doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: Then I'd subtract both our pay and stare at the zero.
S2.fieldNote: The double exposure, her own job and Tomasz's, is what makes this picture so hard for her. She doesn't panic outright because she has a clear ask, government action, and a fallback in her sister. Her pride came through when she talked about asking for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now. I'd want the union and the city sitting down together the first year, not the last. And I'd say it at the school too, because the teachers need to know what they're preparing the kids for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps. Jan would be fifteen, Ola nineteen, so at least Ola would be launched. We could chip away at the mortgage and maybe get a small cushion. But I still don't see where I land, because the work I could move into, like training or grid control, is the same work the AI is coming for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open a savings account the first month and put every callout payment in it. Once I saw other crews doing it, I'd take the company's courses on the new grid systems, in case there's a few years of work supervising machines. Tomasz and I would plan for him to leave driving within two years, maybe into maintenance at the depot. And I'd keep pushing for a public transition fund, because savings alone won't do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel. Not just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ola about her own plans, at nineteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a nurse. Two years ago I'd have said great, solid job. In this picture I'd still tell her to do it, because people want a person with them when they're sick, I think. But I'd tell her not to take on big loans for it. That's where I'd be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said savings alone won't do it. How much do you think you could realistically save in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we're very disciplined, maybe four or five months of expenses. That's more than we've ever had. It buys time to find something, but it doesn't replace two incomes. That's why I keep coming back to the public fund, it's just maths.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, with the union and the city sitting down in the first year. I'd say it at the school too, so teachers know what they're preparing kids for.
S3.think: Five years helps, because our oldest would be launched and we could chip at the mortgage. But I still don't see where I land, since training or grid control is the same work AI is coming for.
S3.do: Opens a savings account in the first month for all callout pay and takes company courses on new grid systems once other crews have. Plans with her partner for him to leave bus driving within two years, and keeps pushing for a public transition fund.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with her hands on the wheel rather than just watching.
S3.quote: It buys time to find something, but it doesn't replace two incomes.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she shifts into planning, and her steady nature shows: she'll take courses once others have proven them. She's honest that savings can't cover the gap and ties her hope to public support. Her advice to her daughter about avoiding big loans was concrete and careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. A decade is long enough to build a real public plan, retraining, income support, all of it. I'd be on the union's working group from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years I can work with. I'd be fifty-three, both kids grown, and the mortgage would be a lot smaller. It's still sad to think of robots in my vaults, but I could see us getting through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an automatic transfer to savings and stick to it for the whole decade. I'd ask to move into training new jointers for the next few years, since that keeps me working while the machines come in. Around year five I'd look seriously at a public-sector job that's harder to automate, maybe something in care or community work, and Tomasz would do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but mostly settled. It feels like something we could plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young jointers you trained, if you knew the end date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest. I'd say: learn this, it'll pay your bills for a few years, but keep one eye on the door. I wouldn't want to train people into a dead end without telling them. That's the union in me, I think, you tell people the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what's the biggest difference for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year one we're on my sister's sofa. In this one, the kids are out of school before it lands, and we've had years to save and move. It's the same robots, but we meet them standing up instead of on our knees.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it, because a decade is long enough for a real public plan. I'd join the union's working group from day one.
S4.think: Ten years I can work with, since I'd be fifty-three with the kids grown and a smaller mortgage. It's sad to picture robots in my vaults, but I could see us getting through.
S4.do: Sets up an automatic transfer to savings for the whole decade and asks to train new jointers for the next few years. Around year five, looks for a public-sector job in care or community work, and her partner does the same.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly settled, because it feels like something they can plan for.
S4.quote: It's the same robots, but we meet them standing up instead of on our knees.
S4.fieldNote: The decade makes a real difference to her mood because both children would be adults and the mortgage smaller. She plans a staged exit, training others first and then moving into care or community work. Her commitment to telling apprentices the truth about the end date stood out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tomasz and I would both lose our jobs in the same year with almost nothing saved. What would help is emergency income from the government that arrives fast, a pause on mortgage payments, and real retraining paid for by the companies making money from all of this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everybody asks about 'the worker', but most families I know have two jobs holding up one roof. If both of ours fall at once, it's not half as bad, it's twice as bad.

headlineQuote: If both of ours fall at once, it's not half as bad, it's twice as bad.
portrait: Uma Kowalski is a 43-year-old underground crew lead for a privatised city electricity company, splicing old high-voltage cable in flooded vaults, with a bus-driver partner, two kids and a mortgage on a flat. She's one of the best jointers in the city but her pay has been frozen for years and the family keeps about two weeks of money in the bank. She uses AI tools now and then and takes up new tech once it's proven. She stays calm if AI fizzles and uneasy, mostly for her partner, in a steady change. Two-year AGI alarms her because both incomes would go at once, while five and ten years let her save, retrain and plan, and she puts her hope in public support and the union.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her partner would lose both their jobs in the same year with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Fast emergency income from the government, a pause on mortgage payments, and real retraining paid for by the companies making money from AI.
